title: Shortest Path in a Binary Matrix: A King Crossing a Blocked Board
summary: Search outward from the start one distance at a time; the first time the far corner comes off the queue, its distance is the shortest.

analogy.scenario: A chess king must cross a 4×4 board from the top-left square to the bottom-right one. Some squares hold other pieces and are blocked. The king moves one square in any of eight directions.

mapping.abstract: A step to one of the 8 neighbors

mapping.real: Squares on the king's route, counting both ends

takeaway.summary: When every move costs the same, BFS reaches cells in order of distance. Record each cell's distance when it's queued; the first time the target comes off the queue, its distance is the answer.
whenToUse: Fewest moves on a grid or graph where every move costs the same
Mazes, boards, and moves with unit cost

scenes.narration: A chess king must cross the board from the top-left square to the bottom-right, moving one square in any of eight directions, around the blocked squares. What's the shortest route?
scenes.caption: A king crosses a board with blocked squares

scenes.narration: Trying every possible route grows explosively. Better to explore close squares before far ones.
scenes.caption: Trying every route explodes

scenes.narration: Start with the king's own square, a route of one square, in the queue. Each square remembers how many squares its route takes.
scenes.caption: Start square: a route of 1 square

scenes.narration: From the corner, five moves fall off the board and two squares are blocked. Only the square to the right is free: distance 2.
scenes.caption: Eight moves: five off the board, two blocked, one free

scenes.narration: From there the king reaches two new squares at once, straight right and diagonally down. Both are distance 3.
scenes.caption: Two new squares at distance 3

scenes.narration: The top-right corner is a dead end. But from the middle square a diagonal slips past the wall to a new square at distance 4.
scenes.caption: A diagonal slips past the wall: distance 4

scenes.narration: One square down is the far corner, distance 5. It joins the queue.
scenes.caption: One more move reaches the far corner: distance 5

scenes.narration: When the corner comes off the queue, every closer square has already come off, so no shorter route exists. The answer is 5.
scenes.caption: The corner comes off the queue: 5 squares

scenes.narration: Free squares are 0 cells, blocked ones are 1s, and king moves are the eight neighbors. BFS expands by distance, so it finds the shortest path in O(n squared) time.
scenes.caption: Squares are cells; moves are 8 neighbors
